summary: SARvis takes NASA’s NISAR radar data and turns it into a 3D map you can interact with, showing how the ground is moving around the world. Press play and watch the change build over time, tap any spot to see its reading and history, and compare NISAR against Sentinel-1 on the same map. The challenge asked for an interactive way to track surface change, so we covered a number of locations around the world.
details:
SARvis app turns NASA’s NISAR L-band radar into an interactive 3D view of how the ground moves at nine places on four continents. Press play to watch the change build over time, tap any spot for its reading and history, and compare NISAR against Sentinel-1 on the same map.

A Python pipeline in Google Colab streams only a crop of each NISAR file, converts radar phase to centimetres, corrects for the ionosphere, and combines two viewing directions into vertical motion. The web app is built with Next.js and MapLibre and hosted on Vercel.

With it we measured a landslide at Portuguese Bend, California, whose fastest spot sank 1.3 m between 5 Dec 2025 and 13 Oct 2026, farmland in California’s Central Valley that sank up to 33 cm as groundwater was pumped, and a 38% to 40% drop in radar signal quality at Destin, Florida, in the passes spanning Hurricane Isaias’s landfall. At Kilauea, Hawaii, our radar results match 15 GPS stations to within about 2 cm.

The benefit is seeing slow hazards with real numbers and dates, without radar training. Available to residents, students and locals. Creative part is showing change as columns that rise from the terrain, on a globe you can fly down from, with a guided demo that explains each piece in plain language. Considered user experience a ton. We want people to enjoy looking and using the app. Polished design to make the user have an intuitive experience, providing the information they were curious about.
